title: Sticky Toffee Pudding
subtitle: Individual steamed date sponge puddings with toffee sauce
excerpt: Dense, dark sponge puddings made with dates and treacle, baked and then drenched in a warm, butter and cream toffee sauce. The most popular British pudding of the past fifty years.

recipe.sourceNotes: Sticky toffee pudding was created in the 1970s, most probably in the Lake District, England. The dish is often attributed to Francis Coulson of the Sharrow Bay Country House Hotel in Ullswater, though its exact origins are disputed. It became one of the most popular restaurant and pub desserts in Britain in the 1980s and 1990s and is now a staple of British menus worldwide. The name is slightly misleading: it is not a steamed pudding in the traditional sense (though it can be steamed) but a baked sponge. The use of dates in the batter is characteristic and provides the distinctive moist, sticky texture. The dates are soaked in boiling water with bicarbonate of soda, which softens them and breaks them down before blending into the batter. The toffee sauce must be poured over the warm puddings and allowed to soak in before serving.

recipeTools.notes: A 12-hole deep muffin tin, or a 20 cm square baking tin for one large pudding.

content.text: Soaking the dates in boiling water with bicarbonate of soda is not optional: the alkali in the bicarbonate breaks down the cell walls of the dates and produces the characteristic dark, soft texture. Blend the soaked dates and liquid to a smooth puree before adding to the batter. The puddings can be made ahead and gently reheated in the microwave; add the hot toffee sauce just before serving.
Heat the oven to 180 C / fan 160 C / gas 4. Pour 200 ml of boiling water over the dates and add the bicarbonate of soda. Leave for 10 minutes, then blend to a smooth puree.
Beat the soft butter and sugar together until fluffy. Beat in the eggs one at a time. Stir in the date puree, black treacle, and vanilla. Fold in the flour and salt.
Butter a 12-hole deep muffin tin. Divide the batter between the holes. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until risen and a skewer comes out clean. Leave in the tin for 5 minutes.

Make the toffee sauce while the puddings bake: melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Add the sugar and cream. Stir until the sugar dissolves, then simmer for 3 minutes until thickened slightly. Turn the puddings out. Pour over the hot toffee sauce and serve immediately with ice cream or clotted cream.
